title: Zelite POC kickoff - capacity & autoscale scoping
summary: POC scoping call to agree success criteria for capacity/autoscale. Discussed workload profiles, latency SLOs, reserved GPU pool sizing, burst capacity, fallback to smaller models, and benchmark plan. Agreed to run two benchmark runs with provided scripts, Redwood to share POC runbook and pricing. Next call scheduled to kick off benchmark.
next_steps: Redwood to share POC runbook, pricing sheet, and benchmark scripts (Chris) by 2025-10-09
Customer to provide sample workload traces and SLO targets (Alex) by 2025-10-10
Schedule benchmark window and cluster access (Maya + Priya) target 2025-10-13
Redwood to provision reserved GPU pool for POC (ops request) after contract signature
action_items: Chris: send POC runbook + pricing + security pointer (due 2025-10-09)
Alex: export 7-day production request histogram and example prompts (due 2025-10-10)
Maya: prepare benchmark scripts and sample config for autoscale thresholds (due 2025-10-11)
Priya: confirm VPC peering/network requirements and provide IP allowlist (due 2025-10-12)
transcript:
[00:00] Chris Baker (Redwood, AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intro, I'm Chris, AE on the account, with Maya our SE. How are you all?
[00:06] Alex Chen (Zelite - Head of ML): Good, thanks. Alex here, Priya on the platform side and Diego joined for the first 10.
[00:12] Maya Patel (Redwood, SE): Hi team. Goal today: scope the POC for capacity and autoscaling, make sure success criteria and benchmarks are clear.
[00:20] Alex: Yeah, we want to validate that Redwood can handle our chat summarization workload at scale, and that costs don't explode.
[00:26] Priya: We have spikes up to ~500 concurrent users during business hours, median request length ~120 tokens, tail up to 2k tokens.
[00:35] Diego (CTO): Also we'd like to see warm pool behavior — cold start latency is a showstopper for us.
[00:41] Maya: Totally. Can you walk me through your traffic shape? Spiky bursts vs steady?
[00:46] Alex: Mostly steady baseline of 200 qps with 5-10 minute spikes to 600 qps. The spikes come in batches, not constant.
[00:55] Chris: Ok, good. For POC we usually provision a reserved GPU pool sized for your baseline and configured burst capacity for spikes. We need to map qps to GPU concurrency.
[01:03] Priya: What's the mapping rule? We use Llama-2 70B-ish, but we can run smaller variants.
[01:09] Maya: Right, so mapping depends on model variant, quantization, and prompting. For example, with a 70B quantized to int8 we see ~25-30 tokens/sec per GPU for long sequences, but for chat prompts with prefix caching effective throughput is higher.
[01:23] Alex: That sounds a bit hand-wavey, we need concrete numbers for the POC.
[01:27] Maya: Understood. For the POC we'll run two benchmark profiles: 1) short chat (median 120 tokens, few-shot), target 95p latency < 600ms; 2) long context summarization (mean 800 tokens), target 95p < 2.5s. We'll instrument both.
[01:44] Speaker 1: Is that 95 percentile or 99?
[01:47] Chris: 95th to start, but we can capture 99th too as part of the benchmark.
[01:52] Priya: For sizing, how many GPUs do you recommend for baseline 200 qps?
[01:58] Maya: If we assume average generation of 120 tokens and batching with continuous KV cache, a rough calc: with a T4-style perf you'd need many, but with A100 or H100 and quantization we estimate 4-6 GPUs for baseline for the smaller variant. For the 70B full model maybe 8-12 depending on perf.
[02:15] Alex: Are you recommending Dedicated reserved GPUs for the POC?
[02:19] Chris: Yes, reserved gives predictable throughput. We can build an autoscale policy that keeps a warm min pool and uses burst capacity for short spikes.
[02:27] Diego: Burst capacity — is that on-demand from hosted pool? What's the SLAs there?
[02:31] Maya: Burst is from shared capacity, it's best-effort but we can set policy: e.g., min=4 reserved, max-burst=+8 from shared, fall back to a smaller model if burst unavailable.
[02:43] Priya: We need deterministic behavior for critical flows. Fallback to smaller model is okay as long as we can guarantee availability and a defined latency envelope.
[02:52] Chris: We'll set explicit fallback policies: primary model -> quantized variant -> smaller model family. We'll also configure canary rollouts.
[02:59] Alex: What about cold starts?
[03:01] Maya: That's where warm pool and cache priming comes in. We recommend keeping a minimum warm GPU pool to keep KV caches hot for your common prefixes. For the POC we'll measure warm vs cold startup times.
[03:13] Speaker 2: Can you capture token-level cost estimates?
[03:15] Chris: Yes we'll include cost per 1M tokens for each config in the pricing sheet.
[03:19] Alex: Benchmarks — what do you need from us?
[03:21] Maya: Sample traces with timestamps and a set of representative prompts, plus target SLOs. We'll run two benchmark windows: one for baseline sizing, one for spike stress test.
[03:32] Priya: How long are windows?
[03:34] Maya: Typically 2-4 hours each, with synthetic load replayed from your traces.
[03:38] Diego: Network: we run in our VPC and need peering. Any special network perf requirements?
[03:43] Maya: We'll need IP allowlist and some egress rules. For latency-sensitive flows we recommend colocating Redwood dedicated in the same region; we'll document the peering steps.
[03:52] Alex: Security — you'll need SOC2 doc and KMS integration info for PII.
[03:56] Chris: We'll share SOC2 summary and KMS integration guide. We can support customer-managed keys in Private deployments as an option.
[04:03] Alex: Timeline? We want benchmarks next week if possible.
[04:06] Chris: We can aim for benchmark window week of 2025-10-13. To do that we need traces and VPC info by 2025-10-10 and agreement on reserved pool sizing.
[04:15] Priya: What are the typical autoscale thresholds? CPU/GPU metrics?
[04:19] Maya: We use request queue length and tokens/sec and GPU utilization signals. For example, scale-up when 95th request queue length > X or GPU util > 65% sustained for 30s; scale-down after cooldown. We'll provide exact config samples.
[04:32] Alex: Can you show us remediation for sustained overloads?
[04:35] Maya: We implement graceful degradation: 1) increase batch size if latency budget allows 2) serve from cached responses 3) fall back to smaller model 4) rate-limit based on priority. We'll include an ordering policy.
[04:49] Diego: Any gotchas on token caching? We saw cache invalidation cause old context issues earlier.
[04:54] Maya: Yes cache correctness is important — we'll show the KV caching TTL and how to prime/flush caches during canary.
[04:59] Chris: For the POC success criteria, propose: 95th latency under 600ms for chat profile and under 2.5s for long profile, cost per 1M tokens below $X (TBD), and system handles 80% of observed spikes without fallback.
[05:14] Alex: 80% sounds reasonable. We'll confirm cost target.
[05:18] Priya: Do you support deterministic model variants? We need consistent outputs for compliance tests.
[05:22] Maya: We'll pin model versions and random seeds for evals, and capture output diffs for regressions.
[05:29] Speaker 1: Can we get a sample autoscale policy?
[05:30] Maya: Yes, I'll upload a sample policy and the benchmark scripts to the shared drive after the call.
[05:36] Chris: Recap: Redwood sends runbook, pricing, SOC2, sample autoscale config. Customer provides traces, VPC info, SLOs. Benchmarks slated week of Oct 13. Next call to schedule benchmark kickoff.
[05:49] Alex: Thanks, that worked well.
[05:51] Priya: One more Q: If burst is unavailable, what's the expected fallback latency?
[05:55] Maya: Depends on model; falling back to smaller model typically reduces latency by ~30-50% but with lower quality. We'll quantify during benchmark.
[06:03] Diego: Ok let's wrap.
[06:05] Chris: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with artifacts.
[06:07] End of recording.
